OCTOBER FIELD LOG — CAT HEAD AREA, LAKE MARION

This is a retrospective of our firsthand October fishing trips, not a claim that the same fish are holding there today. October's fishing gave us a documented starting point for evaluating the seasonal move into November.

OCTOBER 5 — Our trip produced approximately 240 pounds of catfish, including four fish over 50 pounds. Wind was reported around 7 mph from the north-northeast to north-northwest. These are trip totals, not a lakewide catch forecast.

OCTOBER 13 — Fishing near Cat Head, morning surface water temperature was about 75.7°F. Bait was observed in approximately 10–18 feet of water. The recorded catch included a 6-pound channel catfish and an 8-pound blue catfish, followed by a blue reported around 40 pounds later in the trip.

OCTOBER 21 — Near Cat Head, water temperature ranged from approximately 70.3°F to 72.8°F during the trip. We caught blue catfish weighing approximately 30 and 25 pounds in about 18 feet of water, and later a blue around 40 pounds in approximately 22 feet on an upslope.

WHAT THE LOG TELLS US — During the documented October outings, productive water included bait-related structure and depth changes in the upper-teen to low-20-foot range. The October 21 upslope catch shows why the relationship between contours can matter as much as any single depth. These results document where and how we fished on those dates; they do not establish a current bite at Cat Head or across Lake Marion.

NEXT STEP — November coverage will investigate a new location and compare its contours, bait, water conditions, sonar observations and actual fishing results against this October baseline. Public reports explain the general-area structure and reasoning; exact GPS positions and advanced tactics are available to Master Fisherman Patreon supporters.

DIVERSION CANAL FLOW ASSESSMENT — November 10, 2026 (11:35 a.m. EST audit)

STATUS: Current measured Diversion Canal discharge, velocity, direction, and strength NOT independently verified. Santee Cooper's operator feed states last updated November 10, 2026; the latest daily lake elevations and discharge entries are dated November 9, not November 10. Individual lake-gauge observation times and vertical-datum reconciliation are unavailable from the operator's daily table. Do not interpret these figures as simultaneous measured hydraulic head or a direct canal-flow reading.

OPERATOR-REPORTED DAILY LAKE ELEVATIONS (feet; times unspecified): November 9 Lake Marion 74.30, Lake Moultrie 74.19, nominal difference 0.11 ft (Marion higher). November 8 Marion 74.26, Moultrie 74.17, nominal difference 0.09 ft. November 7 Marion 74.25, Moultrie 74.18, nominal difference 0.07 ft. From November 8 to November 9 Marion rose 0.04 ft, Moultrie rose 0.02 ft, and the nominal difference widened 0.02 ft. All are operator-published daily values, NOT independently verified synchronized gauge readings. USGS stations for independent comparison: Marion at Elloree (02169921), Marion at Pineville (02171000), Moultrie at Pinopolis (02172000), and Moultrie at Rediversion (02171635). The datum and timing comparability of these measurements have not been independently established in this audit.

HYDRO OPERATIONS (operator feed updated November 10; schedules tentative): Tuesday November 10 Jefferies Hydro scheduled 3 a.m.–11 p.m.; Wednesday November 11 scheduled 4 p.m.–midnight. St. Stephen Hydro is not scheduled to run either day. The latest facility discharge table is dated November 9 and reports Jefferies 4,748, St. Stephen 0, Spillway Hydro 7, and Spilling 770 (units not independently validated here). These are operator facility entries, not measured Diversion Canal discharge. Neither Jefferies nor St. Stephen schedules demonstrate canal current.

INTERPRETATION — INFERENCE ONLY: If lake elevations are in a common vertical datum and sufficiently contemporaneous, the nominal Marion-higher-than-Moultrie condition is consistent with a potential Marion-to-Moultrie hydraulic gradient. The reported difference increased from 0.09 to 0.11 ft, but no defensible classification of actual canal flow strength or speed follows from that change. Santee Cooper explains that changing Moultrie storage and the lake-to-lake elevation difference influences Diversion Canal flow; this describes general operating mechanics, not today's measured movement. CURRENT CANAL FLOW NOT INDEPENDENTLY VERIFIED.
